overview: The file consists entirely of Department of State list-of-papers and cross-reference sheets indexing records on Japanese aviation law and policy, principally from 1931 through 1939. The indexed correspondence concerns permits and procedures for foreign flights into or across Japan and Japanese-controlled areas, restrictions around fortified zones, unauthorized landings and aerial photography, and enforcement against foreign aviators. Frequently cited cases include Perry Hutton’s Ford Company flight, the Pangborn–Herndon flight, Charles Lindbergh’s possible infringement in the Kuril Islands, and an alleged Pan American Airways overflight of Rota. Later entries address Japan’s Aviation Law, restrictions on international commercial services, creation of a national aviation company, and government regulation of airline tariffs and rates.

subfiles.title: Cross-references on Ford flight permission and Japanese flight instructions
subfiles.about: An internal index sheet points to records concerning Japanese permission for a Ford aircraft’s flight over Manchuria and later instructions governing flights and landing fields in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The first note refers to Japanese insistence that an aviator flying a Ford aircraft from Japan to China by way of Manchuria obtain prior Japanese permission, citing a September 1937 Mukden telegram. The second refers to November 1939 Japanese government instructions concerning flights over Japanese territory and the use of landing fields. Both entries direct researchers to records filed elsewhere in the Department’s decimal system.

subfiles.title: Index of Japanese flight requirements and the Pangborn–Herndon incidents
subfiles.about: This index sheet lists diplomatic records on Japanese requirements for foreign flights and early disputes involving American aviators.
subfiles.summary: The entries summarize Embassy comments on flights across the Kwantung Leased Territory, the South Manchuria Railway Zone, Japan, and Chinese territory, including the case of Perry Hutton and the Ford Company. They also record Eugene Dooman’s discussion with Mr. Tani, Foreign Office stipulations for foreign airmen, and Japanese objections to Pangborn and Herndon landing without permission and photographing fortified zones. The sheet supplies cross-references to related decimal files.

subfiles.title: Index of inquiries and proposed publication on flight procedures
subfiles.about: The sheet indexes efforts to obtain and publish guidance for American airmen flying in Japan, together with records of aviation-law violations.
subfiles.summary: Commerce Department and Aeronautical Chamber of Commerce inquiries sought authoritative information on Japanese flight regulations for American aviators. Other entries concern the Pangborn–Herndon unauthorized landing, a Japanese aviator deprived of a license for violations, and consultation with Japanese authorities over wording proposed for a Commerce Department publication. The final fragment refers to the 1919 Air Navigation Convention and the United States’ position toward it.

subfiles.title: Index of enforcement rules, Lindbergh’s Kuril flight, and published guidance
subfiles.about: This sheet records correspondence about public guidance for American airmen and Japanese enforcement of its aviation regulations.
subfiles.summary: The Commerce Department acknowledged information supplied for a reply to librarian Vera P. Swerig. A separate note reports suspicion that Charles Lindbergh crossed parts of the Kuril Islands without permission, while observing that another aviator might have faced serious consequences. Further entries report Japan’s intention to suspend or prohibit future flights by foreign aviators penalized for violations and add that rule to published guidance on entry into Japanese territory.

subfiles.title: Index of navigation summaries and Japanese commercial-aviation legislation
subfiles.about: This multi-year index sheet covers published guidance, diplomatic updating of national requirements, and interpretation of Japan’s commercial-aviation law.
subfiles.summary: Entries from 1931–1933 concern Commerce Department publication of procedures for American airmen and requests for current summaries of aviation requirements in Japan, China, and Siam; Joseph C. Grew later reported that the Japanese authorities found the summary satisfactory. Two incidental cross-references concern Japanese driving examinations and a failed General Motors–Nielsen Jidosha merger. The 1936 entries address a law restricting international commercial aviation services to Japanese operators, correction of an erroneous digest, and a request for the law’s complete translated text.

subfiles.title: Index of Japan’s Aviation Law, Rota overflight, national airline policy, and rate regulation
subfiles.about: The concluding index sheet points to records on Japanese aviation legislation, an alleged American overflight, and government control of commercial aviation.
subfiles.summary: One entry records the Embassy’s translation of Japan’s Aviation Law and its amendment. Others concern an alleged U.S.-registered aircraft flight over Rota in 1938: Pan American Airways maintained that its aircraft passed north of the island in accordance with instructions to avoid foreign territory and territorial waters, while Japanese authorities requested a warning against repetition. The 1939 entries concern creation of a National Policy Aviation Company, the Japan Aviation Company Law and implementing ordinance, and regulation of airline tariffs and rates.

interest: These sheets are especially useful as a research map: they identify diplomatic correspondence now dispersed across several decimal-file classifications and preserve concise descriptions of records that may otherwise be difficult to locate. They show how civil aviation became entangled with sovereignty, military security, aerial photography, and Japan’s authority in Manchuria and the Pacific islands. The progression from individual overflight disputes in 1931 to national-company formation and tariff regulation in 1939 also documents Japan’s movement toward increasingly centralized control of aviation.
